Tracing & metrics

PCS emits structured tracing events, gated behind one feature flag. pcs-core emits; pcs-service exports.

In one line
Events, a fmt subscriber, and a Prometheus endpoint that carries one series
You need
The tracing feature on pcs-core or pcs-service; the service feature turns it on for you
Read this if
You are wiring a subscriber, picking a RUST_LOG filter, or scraping /metrics and wondering why it is nearly empty

Where instrumentation comes from

Two things leave a running PCS process, and they are wired independently. tracing events go to whatever subscriber you installed. Prometheus metrics go to the /metrics route on the service's HTTP control plane. Neither one feeds the other.

the work being observed emission and export the guest, logging across the seam

The tracing feature

Both crates declare it, and it is off by default in pcs-core (default = ["runtime"]). In pcs-service the service feature includes tracing, and the pcs-service binary requires service, so the shipped binary always has instrumentation compiled in.

TOMLas declared; the service list is abridged
# crates/pcs-core/Cargo.toml
tracing = ["dep:tracing"]

# crates/pcs-service/Cargo.toml
tracing = ["dep:tracing", "pcs-core/tracing"]
service = ["io", "distributed", "tracing", "dep:toml", "dep:axum", ...]
Constraint

This is a compile-time switch, not a runtime one. Every emission site sits inside #[cfg(feature = "tracing")], so with the feature off the call and its field formatting are absent from the binary — there is no disabled-level cost to pay. The corollary is that you cannot turn emission back on without rebuilding.

Two sites keep a fallback for the feature-off build, because losing them silently would be worse than the dependency. HostIo::log falls back to eprintln! so guest log lines are never dropped, and DistributedRunner's claim-release path prints to stderr so a failed release is always visible.

Inside a .wasm guest the feature is never available: pcs-guest pins its dependency as pcs-core = { default-features = false, features = ["guest"] }. A guest reports through the host-io imports instead — log and metric — which the host bridges into its own subscriber.

A guest's println! goes nowhere. The host builds each guest's WASI context with WasiCtxBuilder::new().build() and never calls inherit_stderr(); that builder's documented default is that stdout and stderr eat all input and it does not go anywhere. So println! and eprintln! inside a guest are silently discarded, and host-io::log is the only channel out.

The events, module by module

One span, plus flat events spread across eleven modules. The span is task_attempt, opened once per attempt by the shared retry driver in pcs-core; every attempt of every system in a pipeline stage runs inside one. Field names below are the exact keys the macros record, so they are what you match on in a JSON log pipeline.

TargetLevelsWhat it reports, and with which fields
pcs_core::retry info span, warn, error The task_attempt span at info, carrying attempt (1-based) and max_attempts; a warn per failed-but-retryable attempt with error, attempt, max_attempts, delay_ms; and an error on exhaustion with error and attempts. Both the async and the blocking driver emit it, from one shared attempt counter.
pcs_core::windows::system warn Rows dropped because their timestamp was null: component, time_field, null_count. Needs the windows feature too.
pcs_service::service::standalone info, warn, error Iteration lifecycle and per-source / per-sink failures: iteration, mode, rows_processed, duration_ms, iteration_errors, source_name, sink_name, error. The busiest module, 15 sites.
pcs_service::distributed::runner info, warn, error Expired-lease sweeps and every release-instead-of-ack path: reclaimed_count, claim_id, error.
pcs_service::distributed::consensus::transport::server info, debug, warn The Raft TCP accept loop: addr on bind, peer per connection, error on frame, decode and encode failures.
pcs_service::distributed::parquet_checkpoint debug A parent-directory fsync that failed after a checkpoint write: error. Needs the io feature.
pcs_service::wasm::host_impl trace–error The guest's own host-io::log lines, re-emitted at the level the guest asked for and tagged pipeline and target. A guest host-io::metric call arrives here as a trace event with metric and value.
pcs_service::wasm::runner warn Building the template dataset: describe() failed, or one component's schema would not parse (component, error).
pcs_service::service::http, ::shutdown info, debug, warn, error Control-plane bind and clean shutdown, signal receipt, and the 30-second shutdown budget being exceeded.
pcs_service::commands::serve info, error Binary startup (node_id), which of signal-or-runner-exit fired first, and the exit path.
tower_http::trace info, debug Not PCS code, but it is in the output: build_router installs TraceLayer::new_for_http(), so each request to /health, /ready, /metrics or /status gets a span and request/response events.
One span, not a trace tree

task_attempt is the only span PCS opens. There is no pipeline.run, no pipeline.stage, no system.execute — pipeline/execution.rs carries no instrumentation of its own, so stage boundaries and per-system timings are not visible. Anything that needs a parent-child trace tree, such as OpenTelemetry span export or span-based sampling, has almost nothing to hang information on yet.

Installing a subscriber

PCS never installs a subscriber for you when you use it as a library. Without one, every event is discarded and you see nothing. The minimum is tracing-subscriber with the fmt and env-filter features.

TOMLpath dependencies — these crates are not published
[dependencies]
pcs-core = { path = "../pcs-core", features = ["tracing"] }
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["fmt", "env-filter"] }
Rustinstall once, before the first pipeline runs
use tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(EnvFilter::from_default_env())
        .init();

    // build and run your pipeline; task_attempt spans and any
    // window / runner events now reach stdout
}

The service binary does this for you. pcs-service serve calls init_logging as step 3, before anything else can emit, and treats a second call as an error because the global subscriber is already installed.

Rustwhat the binary calls
use pcs_service::service::config::ObservabilityConfig;
use pcs_service::service::logging::init_logging;

let cfg = ObservabilityConfig::default();  // Pretty format, "info" level
init_logging(&cfg)?;

Level and format from TOML

The [observability] table has exactly two keys. There is no exporter configuration, no sampling ratio, and no per-module table — module filtering is the filter string's job.

TOMLfrom examples/configs/standalone.toml
[observability]
log_format = "pretty"   # use "json" in production log aggregators
log_level = "info"
KeyValuesDefault
log_format "pretty" or "json". Pretty enables ANSI colour only when stdout is a terminal; JSON emits one object per record. "pretty"
log_level Any EnvFilter directive string, so "debug" and "warn,pcs_service::service::standalone=debug" are both valid here. "info"

init_logging turns log_level into the filter pcs=<log_level>,tower_http=info,warn. Directives match the event target by prefix, so the single pcs directive covers both pcs_core::… and pcs_service::…, and everything else in the dependency tree stays at warn.

RUST_LOG wins outright: the environment filter is tried first, and the directive above is only the fallback when RUST_LOG is unset. Both keys can also be overridden per-invocation, by flag or by environment variable.

Bashthree orders of precedence, and real module paths
# CLI flag beats the config file
pcs-service serve --config standalone.toml --log-format json --log-level debug

# ... and so do PCS_LOG_FORMAT / PCS_LOG_LEVEL
PCS_LOG_LEVEL=debug pcs-service serve --config standalone.toml

# RUST_LOG beats all of them: only the standalone runner, everything else quiet
RUST_LOG="warn,pcs_service::service::standalone=info" \
  pcs-service serve --config standalone.toml

# The Raft accept loop, including per-connection debug events
RUST_LOG="warn,pcs_service::distributed::consensus::transport=debug" \
  pcs-service serve --config cluster.toml

# Guest log lines and guest metric calls, nothing else
RUST_LOG="off,pcs_service::wasm::host_impl=trace" \
  pcs-service serve --config standalone_wasm.toml

The Prometheus endpoint

The service binary builds a prometheus::Registry, hands it to opentelemetry_prometheus::exporter(), wraps that in an SdkMeterProvider, installs it as the global OpenTelemetry meter provider, and then describes the standard instruments. The /metrics handler gathers that same registry and encodes it with prometheus::TextEncoder, returning text/plain; version=0.0.4.

Bashdefault bind is 0.0.0.0:8080
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics
# the only series present is pcs_liveness_counter

curl -s localhost:8080/status | jq .standalone
# {
#   "iterations": 7,
#   "rows_processed": 7000,
#   "source_batches_drained": 7,
#   "sink_batches_written": 7,
#   "iteration_errors": 0
# }

/metrics shares the router with /health, /ready and /status, all four behind a 10-second timeout layer. Today /metrics carries a single series, pcs_liveness_counter, recorded once a second by the watchdog task; the other eleven descriptors are covered under what is not instrumented yet. The counters an operator actually wants — iterations, rows, batch and error totals — are on /status instead, read from the runner's own StandaloneStats.

Two of the probes mean less than they look. /ready is flipped to ready immediately after the runner task is spawned, so it reports the process started, not that a pipeline iteration succeeded. And in cluster mode /status always answers "cluster": null, because the service passes no cluster probe into the HTTP state. /health is the one to alert on: it is backed by the watchdog counter, so it goes stale if the main loop wedges.

What is not instrumented yet

Stated plainly, because a metric name in a table is worth nothing if no code writes to it.

  • Eleven of the twelve declared metrics are never emitted. register_standard_metrics only describes instruments — its own doc comment says "Runners increment the counters/gauges; this function only registers descriptions" — and no runner does. Declared but unfed: pcs_pipeline_runs_total, pcs_pipeline_errors_total, pcs_stage_duration_seconds, pcs_source_batches_drained_total, pcs_sink_batches_written_total, pcs_rows_processed_total, pcs_ready, pcs_uptime_seconds, pcs_raft_commit_index, pcs_raft_term, pcs_raft_leader_id. The six counters and the histogram are built and immediately dropped; the observable gauges have no observation callback. Only pcs_liveness_counter is written, by the watchdog.
  • The pipeline execution path emits nothing but retry attempts. task_attempt is the whole story: pipeline/execution.rs has no instrumentation, so there is no event or span at a stage boundary, at a system's start or finish, or on the parallel-stage fan-out.
  • Guest batch metrics are computed and thrown away. The guest fills every field of the WIT run-metrics record — wall-ns, rows-in, rows-out, systems-run, retries — and WasmPipelineRuntime reads only output and checkpoint off the result. Nothing on the host looks at metrics.
  • host-io::metric does not reach Prometheus. The WIT comment says "Host routes to prometheus"; the implementation emits a trace event with metric and value and stops there. A guest counter is a log line, not a series.
  • No OTLP or distributed-trace export. The service depends on opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk with the metrics feature, and opentelemetry-prometheus. tracing-opentelemetry is not a dependency at all, and init_logging installs exactly one EnvFilter plus one fmt layer. You can stack an OTLP layer in your own main when you embed PCS as a library; the shipped binary offers no configuration knob for it.
